title: Grand Theft Auto 6's controversial refuelling action reportedly takes about 10 seconds to perform, which Rockstar's co-studio head says is 'pretty fast for a fill-up'
author: Rick Lane
text:
Every new Rockstar game is more simulation-heavy than the last, and Grand Theft Auto 6 aims to bring players closer to real-life in a variety of ways. One of these is the addition of vehicle refuelling , which will require players to stop off at gas stations (or petrol stations if you're a Brit like me) and watch your disposable income vanish in a stream of fossilised plant matter.
This mechanical tweak has proved somewhat controversial among Grand Theft Auto players, with some believing that refuelling cars will be inconvenient and interrupt the flow of driving and shooting the series is built upon. Yet while Rockstar is sticking to its guns on the matter of refuelling, co-studio head Rob Nelson recently stated that filling up your car won't be a massive drag on your adventure across Vice City.
Nelson's comments come via YouTuber TGG (via GamesRadar+ ) who recently saw an extended preview of Rockstar's hotly anticipated crime sim, which included refuelling in action. TGG says that gas stations allow players to both repair and refuel cars, and facilitate recharging for electric vehicles alongside refuelling for cars powered by internal combustion engines. Selecting the refuel/recharge option triggers a refuelling cutscene that TGG says lasts around 10 seconds.
The preview was apparently overseen by Nelson, who commented on the refuelling during play. "Hey, that's pretty fast for a fill up," Nelson observed when getting gas. "You can't complain about that." It also appears there is some trepidation within Rockstar about the refuelling, as when discussing the system with TGG, Nelson stated. "We'll see what people say," before asking "Do you think people are going to like it?"
For his part, TGG reckons that "Fuel isn't really going to be an issue unless you're not thinking about what you're doing". And I think this is probably going to be the case for most people unless Rockstar makes the need to refuel too frequent. When Red Dead Redemption 2 arrived in 2018, some players complained about the simulation-heavy elements of that, like how Arthur Morgan moved and having to fiddle around with your saddlebags for inventory management.

title: Gaming monitors are one of the only good things about PC hardware right now, but one niche feature is underloved
author: James Bentley
text:
The memory crisis may be in full swing, taking numerous PC components with it, but the value of gaming monitors is one of a few hardware things that has actually improved over the last few years. In fact, their price-to-quality ratio is kind of outrageous right now, with even relatively recent QD-OLED screens going for around $300 .
As such, monitors are one of the few things I check over without rolling my eyes, and therefore, they're one of a handful of techie bits that actually excites me. But that doesn't mean even they can't improve; when I chatted to gaming monitor brand AOC a few months ago, even its designers are aware the software isn't up to snuff.
I've been testing out the Koorui G2741L, a dual mode 4K/1080p monitor, over the last few weeks, and all I can think is 'gosh, why aren't more companies doing dual mode,' and 'why aren't more companies doing dual mode better ?'
The central argument for dual mode makes so much sense to me. When you want your games to look pretty, you swap to 4K at a lower refresh rate, and when you want something snappy and competitive, you drop it to 1080p with a much higher refresh rate. You can get dual mode monitors like this Acer Nitro 4K/1080p one for as cheap as $160 , they're even pretty reasonably priced right now (even if the 4K refresh rate is a pretty tiny 72 Hz).
(Image credit: Future) Sure, you can technically just swap the resolution of your monitor at any time, but dual mode gives you access to a max refresh rate that is above what you would get if you just turned down the resolution of a 4K monitor.
But dual mode monitors have a few problems. For one, the thing I spotted instantly with the Koorui is that the swap between 4K and 1080p is a tad slow. The swap happens with a physical button, and in the case of the Koorui, it's a series of physical buttons. These navigate through the monitor's built-in software to then switch modes. It also just takes a while to swap, and the more seconds it adds, the less convenient it feels.
Another problem with dual mode monitors is the added blur. 1080p on a dual mode monitor tends to look worse than 1080p on a 1080p native screen. The reason 4K dual mode monitors go down to 1080p is that dual mode traditionally reduces the resolution to a quarter while doubling the refresh rate (though some monitors now triple or quadruple the refresh rate ).
Most gaming monitors seem to use some sort of interpolation algorithm. Our Jeremy said in his Asus ROG Strix XG27UCG review , "You wouldn't want to use this monitor's 1080p mode on the desktop. It's a little soft and blurry. However, in-game it actually works pretty well and is certainly preferable to 1080p interpolated in the normal fashion onto a 4K panel."
(Image credit: Future) Gaming monitor companies do have the ability to make better dual mode monitors. The Alienware AW2725QF opts for a form of pixel doubling (doubling up pixels in both vertical and horizontal directions), getting you much closer to a 'native 1080p' resolution. This is called integer scaling.
So, right now, if you buy a dual mode monitor, you are likely making a compromise on the lower of the two resolutions. But even with that downside, I'd take a 4K desktop experience and 4K gaming in singleplayer games, then 1080p for competitive games over 4K for absolutely everything.
There's plenty of room for dual mode monitors to grow. Just look at how far OLEDs have come since their inception: Burn-in has become far less of a problem, and LG's latest RGB Stripe panel has effectively killed font fringing. Not only could interpolation algorithms get better, but integer scaling could become more commonplace with the growth of the dual mode market.
(Image credit: Future) The same could be said for the process of actually swapping modes. The ability to swap between resolutions could benefit from being snappier and easier to access. I'd personally love a single button that makes the swap in just a moment. And I'd also love that the biggest downside of swapping to 1080p is simply the resolution, and no other artifacting or blur.
But even now, with its flaws, I quite like dual mode. 1080p for some gaming on a dual mode monitor, even with plain 'ol interpolation, works well enough, and 4K for a standard desktop experience isn't such a resource hog that I'd want 1080p for it anyway.
I particularly like the fact that the price point has become so good on dual mode monitors that it's almost just an added bonus, and not something you specifically pay more for. As even OLEDs are becoming downright reasonably priced, I'd love for dual mode to get the love it deserves. Now, a value-oriented dual mode OLED monitor with integer scaling and good software? That's the dream.

title: This free lockpicking puzzler you can play in your browser is unexpectedly one of the most thrilling games I've encountered this year
author: Rick Lane
text:
I love lockpicking minigames, especially when representatively they're as far away from the act of lockpicking as possible. While I admire the elegance of Bethesda's bobby-pin/screwdriver system seen in Fallout 4 , I'm much more interested in the weirder solutions like Splinter Cell 's baffling pin-flicking system, or Gothic Remake 's absurdly elaborate sliding puzzle system.
I love how developers have tried so many ways to represent the act of lockpicking, and that despite this nobody has 'solved' the problem of virtual lockpicking yet (though Bethesda has arguably come closest). Inevitably, then, I was drawn to the idea of a game that is all about lockpicking. But I never expected that it could be as imaginative and thrilling as Lockpicks-11 .
An entry for Ludum Dare 57, Lockpicks-11 places you in the role of an unnamed thief in the middle of a heist. Yet rather than being a fully fledged burglary simulator like Thief, Lockpicks-11 distils the act of larceny to a linear sequence of locked doors.
What makes Lockpicks-11 interesting is that every lock is wildly different. Some are based upon recognisable locking mechanisms, like inputting a four digit code, or aligning symbols via a tumbler system. Others are more out there, like replicating a sequence of musical notes, or navigating a 2D maze to collect objects.
The order of these puzzles is randomised each time you play, and Lockpicks-11 provides minimal context to how each puzzle works, so you have to figure it out for yourself. On top of that, your thief is being chased by the world's slowest security guard, and if he catches you before you unlock a door, it's game over.
This combination of elements—the puzzles, the randomisation, the lack of context, and the timed element—makes Lockpicks-11 shockingly tense. The maze puzzle, for example, randomises the controls for navigating the maze, and in my last run I was seconds from being caught before I snatched the last collectible and my knotted fingers prised open the lock.
For a game built in 72 hours by a team of two, it's a mightily impressive creation. If you fancy giving Lockpicks-11 yourself, you can play it in your browser. If you're a lockpicking aficionado like myself, I'd also recommend you check out The Museum of Mechanics: Lockpicking , a digital exhibit that explores the history and evolution of these security-busting minigames.

title: Half of France's premier FPS sibling duo just put out the most exhilarating parkour game I've ever played, and it's only $8
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
Weird Weekend
Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Ted, and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager .
Vholume is not big on waypoints or barriers, and I love it for that. In the first level, there's a naturalistic, reasonably signposted "correct" path to walk you through the tutorial. I immediately went the opposite direction for shiggles to indulge my well-honed sense of childlike wonder and curiosity. I lost myself in a field of brutalist rooftops, wallrunning and mantling about with no sign of the beaten path in sight. I accidentally stumbled across the level secret this way, unlocking a B-side bonus mission.
My wanderlust eventually intersected with the critical path, and after wrapping the tutorial, I unlocked time trial mode for this level. After my super-chill freeform exploration, white knuckling it to a gold level time almost felt like a completely different game.
Alongside co-developers Nathan Grange and Niels Tiercelin, Vholume was created by Léonard Lemaitre, one half of the brotherly duo behind our 2024 FPS of the year, Straftat . This previous work was an atomically pure arena shooter, like Quake 3 by way of the Source engine. It was all about lightning-quick rounds and movement mastery, with a dry, slapstick sense of humor.
Vholume borrows Straftat's surreal, dreamlike sensibility, and builds on its movement toolbox, adding an insanely good wall run to the wall jumps and crouch slide. Even with the similar DNA, it's a very different kind of game. There's a multiplayer mode, but the focus is singleplayer time trial and exploration amid desolate concrete cityscapes.
The vibes and music are mournful, but the platforming is pure goddamn speed force momentum, all but blasting you back in your chair. Trying to think of other games that feel this propulsive , what came to mind for me were F-Zero GX and Neon White . Counter-Strike surf maps and the defrag mod for Quake are also handy points of comparison (and possible inspiration.)
Slide city
The more time I've put into Vholume, the more defrag feels like the most relevant comparison. You can do sexy cinematic parkour if you want, but the real shit is crouch slide bunny hopping to get crazy momentum for PB level times. There are already speedrunners like Fobxx on YouTube showing off blistering world record level clears.
I love that Vholume doesn't put a mechanical damper on its movement tools: I can crouch slide bunny hop till my heart's content, and this is probably one of the most generous wallrun durations I've seen in a platformer. You know how some games say you can only wall jump so many times before your feet have to touch the ground again? None of that here.
Instead, Vholume limits your abuse of these mechanics through level design. This game was made with an insanely fast, mobile protagonist in mind. One trick I love is how Vholume will space out platforms or drops just so to punish heedless hopping.
There will be irregular distances between a series of platforms so you risk overshooting one or falling just short of another if you're button mashing. Elsewhere, gaps you have to crouch slide through will be deliberately placed to bring a sloppy, mis-timed bunnyhop sequence to a standstill, forcing the humiliating ritual of slowly crouch walking under instead.
IronEqual IronEqual IronEqual IronEqual IronEqual IronEqual Speed and precision are the name of the game. If that sounds too stressful, I think Vholume more than offers full value as a casual, exploration-forward platformer and mood piece. But man, when you really get moving it is positively thrilling. Even though it costs more than Straftat's hard-to-beat "free," at $8, Vholume is firmly a "no duh" purchase recommendation in my book.

title: Confession time: Alright, come clean—how tidy are your bags in your MMOs?
author: Harvey Randall
text:
Terminally Online
(Image credit: Future) This is Terminally Online : PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice.
Ah, the MMO inventory. The delightful abstraction that means we don't need to actually think all that hard about where to store the hundreds of thousands of pelts, steaks, teeth, claws, trinkets, coins, crystals, and so-on that we accrue. Our bags are full of crap, it is tradition .
On the one hand, I'm grateful for it. I'm out here to grind and run dungeons, not try to Jenga-stack a briefcase Resident Evil-style. On the other hand, good lord does my head spin every time I open up my inventory and gaze upon the horrors of my own chronic lack of organisation. I despair. Please don't tell people how I live.
(Image credit: Square Enix) I could argue that it's the game's fault. Giving me an auto-sorting feature means I can endure a descent into of disorganisation without much trouble. At the very least, if I click a button, all of my junk will be organised by type. Often, these systems aren't how I'd do it. For instance, I'd love it if all the gear I'm de-synthing in FF14 could stop being in the initial inventory slots. But they're still useful.
And yet I don't represent the majority of all MMORPG players (despite my best efforts, I'm still working on the hive mind thing). And neither do you, statistically speaking—these are games frequented by millions of players, and I'm not that smug to assume this column is that popular.
However, I would like to get an idea of how tidy Terminally Online readers are. After all, we know you're fashionable, like your keybinds, and mostly healers . So please, satisfy my curiosity: Are your bags full of junk, or have you sorted your demicrystalised megalized torment orbs or whatever by both colour and patch release date?
Or, are you utterly lost in heaps of garbage like I am. And hey, maybe that's part of the charm—after all, there was a time where an MMO's inconvenience was part of the experience .

Terminally Online

This is Terminally Online: PC Gamer's very own MMO column. Every other week, I'll be sharing my thoughts on the genre, interviewing fellow MMO-heads like me, taking a deep-dive into mechanics we've all taken for granted, and, occasionally, bringing in guest writers to talk about their MMO of choice.

Ah, the MMO inventory. The delightful abstraction that means we don't need to actually think all that hard about where to store the hundreds of thousands of pelts, steaks, teeth, claws, trinkets, coins, crystals, and so-on that we accrue. Our bags are full of crap, it is tradition.

On the one hand, I'm grateful for it. I'm out here to grind and run dungeons, not try to Jenga-stack a briefcase Resident Evil-style. On the other hand, good lord does my head spin every time I open up my inventory and gaze upon the horrors of my own chronic lack of organisation. I despair. Please don't tell people how I live.

I could argue that it's the game's fault. Giving me an auto-sorting feature means I can endure a descent into of disorganisation without much trouble. At the very least, if I click a button, all of my junk will be organised by type. Often, these systems aren't how I'd do it. For instance, I'd love it if all the gear I'm de-synthing in FF14 could stop being in the initial inventory slots. But they're still useful.

And yet I don't represent the majority of all MMORPG players (despite my best efforts, I'm still working on the hive mind thing). And neither do you, statistically speaking—these are games frequented by millions of players, and I'm not that smug to assume this column is that popular.

However, I would like to get an idea of how tidy Terminally Online readers are. After all, we know you're fashionable, like your keybinds, and mostly healers. So please, satisfy my curiosity: Are your bags full of junk, or have you sorted your demicrystalised megalized torment orbs or whatever by both colour and patch release date?

Or, are you utterly lost in heaps of garbage like I am. And hey, maybe that's part of the charm—after all, there was a time where an MMO's inconvenience was part of the experience.

Best MMOs: Most massive
Best strategy games: Number crunching
Best open world games: Unlimited exploration
Best survival games: Live craft love
Best horror games: Fight or flight

title: 群星集结海岛逐浪，9月11日《PEL奇遇时光三亚篇》斗鱼直播重磅开启
text:
PEL夏季赛圆满收官，赛场烽烟落幕，电竞热爱永不降温。9月11日，由斗鱼与《和平精英》联合推出的电竞直播综艺《PEL奇遇时光三亚篇》将正式开启。本次直播内容集结超强全明星阵容，PEL明星选手带队，斗鱼平台头部主播及优质电竞KOL齐聚三亚，将在碧海椰林之间展开一场持续四天的海岛竞技之旅。
PEL全明星阵容齐聚三亚，海岛冒险之旅启程
《PEL奇遇时光三亚篇》将由TEC·33Svan、深圳STE·芷田、杭州KSG.吒宝、杭州LGD·猫猫四位PEL职业选手带队，集结职业选手、斗鱼主播、电竞KOL、专业主持多重圈层嘉宾，在椰林海风间组队迎接各类挑战，阵容含金量拉满，队员间的化学反应值得期待！
浙江RSG无痕、福州NV·Ydd、4AM·mingskr、LTG魏无羡、TJB·白小纯等一众实力人气PEL职业选手；惜兮未曦CCVC、若若跑的贼快、艾琳、百变姑姑肖淑洁等斗鱼平台头部人气主播；Dy花老湿、苏哲、武子弈、幸福等知名KOL及PEL专业主持小鱼也将全程参与，全员齐聚三亚，解锁沉浸式海岛奇遇电竞之旅。
四天高强度挑战自我，冒险奖杯花落谁家？
9月11日-14日的四天时间里，嘉宾们将参加神秘?“P岛主”特设的奇遇冒险杯赛，以组别为单位展开“奇遇冒险杯”的竞技之旅。赛程层层递进，分别从团队协作、体力意志、综合素养与全局策略四大维度展开角逐，搭配阶梯式现金的奖励方式，充分调动每位嘉宾的竞技热情与胜负欲。
9月11日开播首日，全体嘉宾正式集结三亚，开启破冰互动，通过雷神小赛、PEL团队运动会等趣味比拼，快速拉近队员距离，凝聚团队默契。值得一提的是，队员中将安排三名卧底全程隐匿身份完成专属任务，四天赛程里卧底是否被成功识破揪出，也将直接左右最终战队成绩与比赛结果。
次日，四大战队将迎来体能与意志的试炼，以海上5KM接力赛为重头戏，沙滩热身、室内游戏及和平精英手游对抗赛轮番登场，从体能挑战到电竞赛场，全方位考验选手的爆发力、耐力与临场抗压能力。第三日则继续跳出传统电竞赛场，以趣味料理王大赛为核心，考验各战队的统筹规划能力、团队配合度与临场创意，解锁选手与主播赛场之外的不同魅力。
收官日将在水上乐园开启终极策略博弈，迎来卧底指认环节，最终决出本次奇遇冒险之旅的“精英冒险队”。紧张刺激的竞技对抗过后，松弛治愈的全员狂欢之夜将为整场活动画上圆满句号。直播期间，平台还将开放在线投票通道，观众可自主投票选择挑战内容，全程参与节目进程，让每一轮比拼都充满未知与惊喜，大幅提升节目互动性与观赏性。
此前，斗鱼《和平精英冒险之旅》已先后走过长白山、阿勒泰、舟山等地，邀请选手、主播们来到线下，结合地域特色推出了一系列内容丰富的直播节目。本次落地三亚，《PEL奇遇时光三亚篇》内容升级，平台继续发挥以游戏为核心的社区优势、主播生态及内容运营能力，通过优质PGC内容持续深化厂商合作，并为广大电竞爱好者带来更加新鲜有趣的内容体验。
当“特种兵”化身“冒险家”，嘉宾们将在椰风海韵里碰撞出怎样的新鲜火花？9月11日至9月14日，锁定斗鱼官方直播间【9209119】，全程见证这场南国奇遇冒险！
